title: Work in Progress: Middleware-Transparent Callback Enforcement in Commoditized Component-Oriented Real-time Systems
summary:
Real-time scheduling in commoditized component-oriented real-time systems,
such as ROS 2 systems on Linux, has been studied under nested scheduling: OS
thread scheduling and middleware layer scheduling (e.g., ROS 2 Executor).
However, by establishing a persistent one-to-one correspondence between
callbacks and OS threads, we can ignore the middleware layer and directly apply
OS scheduling parameters (e.g., scheduling policy, priority, and affinity) to
individual callbacks. We propose a middleware model that enables this idea and
implements CallbackIsolatedExecutor as a novel ROS 2 Executor. We demonstrate
that the costs (user-kernel switches, context switches, and memory usage) of
CallbackIsolatedExecutor remain lower than those of the MultiThreadedExecutor,
regardless of the number of callbacks. Additionally, the cost of
CallbackIsolatedExecutor relative to SingleThreadedExecutor stays within a
fixed ratio (1.4x for inter-process and 5x for intra-process communication).
Future ROS 2 real-time scheduling research can avoid nested scheduling,
ignoring the existence of the middleware layer.

title: Recasting Experimental Constraints on Relativistic Magnetic Monopoles
summary:
Magnetic monopoles with masses up to $10^{14}$ GeV can be accelerated to
relativistic velocities in Galactic and intergalactic magnetic fields. The
cosmic flux of relativistic monopoles is constrained by various experiments,
with the limits given as functions of the monopole velocity (Lorentz factor) at
the detectors. The velocity, however, is usually treated as a free parameter
due to the ambiguity in the computation of the acceleration before the
monopoles arrive at Earth. We explicitly evaluate the velocity by exploiting
recent studies on cosmic magnetic fields and the monopole acceleration therein,
to recast experimental limits in terms of the mass of monopoles. By applying
our method to various terrestrial experiments, including the Pierre Auger
Observatory, IceCube, MACRO, and the upcoming Cherenkov Telescope Array
Observatory, as well as to astrophysical constraints, we report limits on the
flux of monopoles for a wide range of monopole masses. We also highlight the
role of monopoles as messengers of cosmic magnetic fields, and discuss the
possibility of using monopole experiments to probe intergalactic magnetic
fields.

title: Scaling Data Center TCP to Terabits with Laminar
summary:
Laminar is the first TCP stack designed for the reconfigurable match-action
table (RMT) architecture, widely used in high-speed programmable switches and
SmartNICs. Laminar reimagines TCP processing as a pipeline of simple
match-action operations, enabling line-rate performance with low latency and
minimal energy consumption, while maintaining compatibility with standard TCP
and POSIX sockets. Leveraging novel techniques like optimistic concurrency,
pseudo segment updates, and bump-in-the-wire processing, Laminar handles the
transport logic, including retransmission, reassembly, flow, and congestion
control, entirely within the RMT pipeline.
  We prototype Laminar on an Intel Tofino2 switch and demonstrate its
scalability to terabit speeds, its flexibility, and robustness to network
dynamics. Laminar reaches an unprecedented 25M pkts/sec with a single host core
for streaming workloads, enough to exceed 1.6Tbps with 8K MTU. Laminar delivers
RDMA-equivalent performance, saving up to 16 host CPU cores versus the TAS
kernel-bypass TCP stack with short RPC workloads, while achieving 1.3$\times$
higher peak throughput at 5$\times$ lower 99.99p tail latency. A key-value
store on Laminar doubles the throughput-per-watt versus TAS. Demonstrating
Laminar's flexibility, we implement TCP stack extensions, including a sequencer
API for a linearizable distributed shared log, a new congestion control
protocol, and delayed ACKs.

\title{Scaling Data Center TCP to Terabits with \sys{}}
\author{Rajath Shashidhara}
\affiliation{\institution{University of Washington}\city{}\country{}}
\author{Antoine Kaufmann}
\affiliation{\institution{MPI-SWS}\city{}\country{}}
\author{Simon Peter}
\affiliation{\institution{University of Washington}\city{}\country{}}



\begin{abstract}
  \sys{} is the first TCP stack designed for the reconfigurable match-action
  table (RMT) architecture, widely used in high-speed programmable switches and
  SmartNICs.\ \sys{} reimagines TCP processing as a pipeline of simple
  match-action operations, enabling line-rate performance with low latency and
  minimal energy consumption, while maintaining compatibility with standard TCP
  and POSIX sockets. Leveraging novel techniques like optimistic concurrency,
  pseudo segment updates, and bump-in-the-wire processing, \sys{} handles the
  transport logic, including retransmission, reassembly, flow, and congestion
  control, entirely within the RMT pipeline.

  We prototype \sys{} on an Intel Tofino2 switch and demonstrate its
  scalability to terabit speeds, its flexibility, and robustness to network
  dynamics.\ \sys{} reaches an unprecedented 25M pkts/sec with a single host
  core for streaming workloads, enough to exceed 1.6Tbps with 8K MTU\@. \sys{}
  delivers RDMA-equivalent performance, saving up to 16 host CPU cores versus
  the TAS kernel-bypass TCP stack with short RPC workloads, while achieving
  1.3$\times$ higher peak throughput at 5$\times$ lower 99.99p tail latency. A
  key-value store on \sys{} doubles the throughput-per-watt versus TAS\@.
  Demonstrating \sys{}'s flexibility, we implement TCP stack extensions,
  including a sequencer API for a linearizable distributed shared log, a new
  congestion control protocol, and delayed ACKs.
\end{abstract}
 




\maketitle


\section{Introduction}



Cheap, versatile, and high-performance networking is essential for scaling data
centers to support billions of users across interactive cloud applications, big
data analytics, and emerging AI workloads. Even as network hardware scales to
terabit speeds to meet these demands, software-based TCP stacks struggle to
keep pace, leading to inefficiencies in bandwidth utilization, energy
consumption, and processing overhead. This efficiency challenge is further
amplified by the growing adoption of compute-constrained SmartNICs for
orchestrating data movement across high-bandwidth accelerators and
disaggregated resource pools~\cite{lovelock,io_server,gimbal,beehive}. Even
with state-of-the-art kernel-bypass TCP stacks, applications spend up to 48\%
of the per-packet CPU cycles in the stack~\cite{flextoe}, while TCP stacks
designed for programmable network processing units (NPUs)~\cite{flextoe} and
FPGAs~\cite{tonic,beehive} present limitations in scalability, complexity, and
energy efficiency. Scaling these solutions to higher bandwidths efficiently
remains elusive.






On the other hand, ASIC-based transport stacks, including TCP offload engines
(TOEs) and remote direct memory access (RDMA), are highly efficient, but
specialized and inflexible. For example, the Chelsio Terminator TOE optimizes
bulk flows and performs poorly for RPCs~\cite{flextoe}, while RDMA over
converged Ethernet (RoCE) presents operational challenges in the
cloud~\cite{1rma,zeronic,bai2023empowering}. Both are largely confined to
specialized high-performance computing and storage
deployments~\cite{bai2023empowering,roce_ai}.




To bridge this gap, we explore the reconfigurable match-action table (RMT)
architecture~\cite{metamorphosis}. Deployed in high-speed programmable network
switches~\cite{tofino2} and SmartNICs~\cite{pensando_elba}, RMT has emerged as
a promising architecture for flexible packet
processing~\cite{conweave,rmtalloc,rmtfairq,bfc,pegasus,mind,concordia,redplane,tea}.
RMT offers line-rate packet processing via sequential match-action stages with
limited local state and strict timing. However, implementing TCP in RMT is
challenging: TCP requires complex state updates with intricate dependencies,
consistent state for bidirectional flow coordination, and buffering for
segments awaiting reassembly and acknowledgement. All are ill-suited to RMT’s
unidirectional pipeline that restricts state dependencies, limited feedback
mechanisms that complicate consistency, and no in-pipeline buffering.



We present \sys{}, the first TCP stack tailored to the RMT architecture,
enabling practical TCP processing at terabit speeds without compromising
line-rate throughput, low latency, energy efficiency, or flexibility.\ \sys{}
reimagines TCP as a pipeline of lightweight match-action operations, enabling
one-shot, line-rate processing without buffering. To address RMT’s key
constraints, \sys{} introduces:
\begin{enumerate*}[label={(\arabic*)}]
  \item optimistic concurrency with deferred validation, performing fast-path
        speculative updates validated downstream, to handle dependencies on
        state further down the line;
  \item pseudo segment injection to effect updates to state variables in prior
        stages, resolving cyclic state dependencies without side-effects or
        stalling the pipeline; and
  \item a bump-in-the-wire design that eliminates recirculation and performs
        stateful TCP processing in a single pipeline pass.
\end{enumerate*}
Together, these principles enable terabit-scale performance, while maintaining
TCP semantics, POSIX socket compatibility, and energy efficiency.






We make the following contributions:

\begin{compactitem}[\labelitemi]
  \item We present the design of \sys{}, describing how to overcome the
        challenges of mapping stateful protocols to programmable hardware with
        limited resources and timing. By addressing these challenges, \sys{}
        informs efficient design of next-generation transport stacks, including
        on SmartNICs, FPGAs, and hybrid systems that integrate programmable and
        fixed-function components.


  \item We prototype \sys{} on an Intel Tofino2
        switch~\cite{tofino2,netberg_aurora810}. With \sys{}'s design
        principles, we are the first to demonstrate the viability of the RMT
        architecture for building a TCP stack rivaling ASIC performance and
        energy efficiency, while remaining flexible. We will open-source
        \sys{}.

  \item We compare \sys{} to Linux, the TAS~\cite{tas} kernel-bypass TCP stack,
        and RDMA (\shortsecref{sec:eval}).\ \sys{} surpasses TAS's peak
        throughput using 16 fewer CPU cores, delivering RDMA equivalent
        performance and efficiency.\ \sys{} reaches an unprecedented 25\,Mpps
        per-core for streaming workloads, enough to saturate 1.6Tbps with 8K
        MTU\@. A key-value store on \sys{} achieves 2$\times$
        throughput-per-watt while maintaining a 99.99p tail latency lower than
        TAS's best case latency.\ \sys{} is POSIX sockets compatible,
        interoperates well with other network stacks, and is resilient to
        packet loss and congestion, achieving up to 1.3$\times$ higher
        throughput than TAS under low packet loss rates. We showcase \sys{}'s
        flexibility by integrating an in-network sequencer, similar to
        NoPaxos~\cite{nopaxos} and accelerating a shared log to achieve
        line-rate with a single core. We also implement extensions, such as
        Timely congestion control and delayed ACKs.
\end{compactitem}
 \section{Background}

We survey existing flexible TCP stack architectures, evaluating their
scalability and efficiency (\shortsecref{sec:arch-survey}). Next, we provide
background on the match-action architecture, detailing its core processing
characteristics and mechanisms that enable high-speed programmable packet
processing (\shortsecref{sec:rmt-architecture}). Finally, we identify and
discuss key challenges associated with implementing a stateful TCP stack on
this architecture, specifically issues arising from RMT's pipeline constraints,
consistency requirements, and limited resource availability
(\shortsecref{sec:rmt-challenges}).

\subsection{Existing Flexible TCP Stack Architectures}\label{sec:arch-survey}


Numerous proposals re-architect the TCP stack to accelerate packet processing,
while retaining flexibility, either purely on general-purpose CPUs or by
leveraging programmable hardware architectures, like network processing units
(NPUs) and field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). Unfortunately, none of these
can efficiently scale to terabits.


\paragraph{Sequential}
Conventional software-based TCP stacks, including the Linux in-kernel TCP
stack, and the TAS kernel-bypass stack employ a sequential architecture where a
single thread fully executes the TCP processing for each segment of a
connection~\cite{cai2021understanding,tas}. Scalability is achieved by
distributing connections across threads, with hardware-assisted flow steering
for load balancing.
While simple, this design limits per-connection processing bandwidth to
single-core performance.


\paragraph{Data-parallel pipeline}
To alleviate this bottleneck, recent proposals~\cite{snap, netchannel, flextoe}
decompose the TCP stack into a data-parallel execution pipeline, comprising of
distinct modules for handling DMA, scheduling, header processing, API, and
transport logic.
The granularity of parallelism in these proposals is limited by stragglers
created by variability in per-core processing times and inter-core queueing. In
the end, TCP transport logic remains a single module (cf.~\emph{Protocol}
module in FlexTOE~\cite{flextoe}) that serializes per-connection processing.



\paragraph{Circuit}
FPGA-based TCP stack proposals largely implement per-connection processing in
circuits, within a single clock cycle. For instance, Tonic~\cite{tonic}
implements the entire TCP transport logic on an FPGA to meet a 10ns timing
constraint, sufficient to saturate 100Gbps with 128 B packets. Higher
bandwidths necessitate further reduction in clock cycle duration, posing a
significant design challenge, which persists for any flexible enhancement.
FPGAs at high clock frequency are also power-intensive, rivaling the power
consumption of CPUs.





\subsection{Match-Action Architecture}\label{sec:rmt-architecture}





The reconfigurable match-action table (RMT) architecture is optimized for
line-rate packet processing. It leverages the parallelism inherent in network
packet processing, enabling simultaneous packet header operations, and a
pipeline to chain dependent operations via multiple stages. This design has
demonstrated bandwidths exceeding 6 billion packets per second at only
\textasciitilde{} 400 ns of latency, as well as power consumption comparable to
ASICs~\cite{metamorphosis, netberg_aurora810}. In this section, we describe a
typical RMT architecture, found in switches and SmartNICs.


\paragraph{Processing characteristics}
Any RMT program operates at the maximum packet processing bandwidth of the
pipeline, sufficient to saturate line rate, even with small packets
(\textasciitilde{} 128B in typical implementations).
RMT pipeline stages have a fixed processing latency and operate in lock-step.
Thus, the pipeline has a fixed aggregate processing latency (typically a few
hundred nanoseconds) determined at compile-time, based on the number of stages
utilized by the program.
Network packets enter the RMT processing pipeline via a MAC or DMA input
channel. Processing begins with a programmable parser extracting responsive
packet fields into a Packet Header Vector (PHV).
The PHV then passes through multiple pipeline stages, consisting of programmable arithmetic-logic units (ALUs) that can
simultaneously act on several PHV fields using primitive arithmetic operations,
based on matching PHV fields. For maintaining state across packets, the only
available memory is local to each pipeline stage.
After processing, a deparser recombines the PHV with the packet.

\paragraph{Traffic manager}
RMT implementations typically partition the pipeline into ingress and egress,
with a traffic manager (TM) in-between (cf. Figure~\ref{fig:highlevel-arch}).
The TM may temporarily buffer packets, such as during traffic bursts, and it
schedules packets to the egress pipeline, matching pipeline and channel
bandwidth constraints. The TM enables lossless egress operation by responding
to backpressure mechanisms, such as Ethernet pause frames and PCIe flow
control.









\paragraph{Additional processing mechanisms.}
RMT supports several mechanisms to trigger further processing and to carry
state back into the pipeline:
\begin{compactenum}[\labelitemi]
  \item \textbf{Recirculation.} RMT implementations typically incorporate a
  recirculation channel, enabling multiple passes through the pipeline.
  However, each pass reduces the effective bandwidth of the RMT pipeline and
  doubles its latency, making this mechanism infeasible for line-rate
  processing.
  \item \textbf{Mirroring.} The deparser may generate copies of a PHV
  and reinject them at the TM\@. Each mirrored PHV is scheduled separately by
  the TM and may be further modified in egress. Mirroring also reduces effective
  RMT bandwidth, but much less than recirculation, as only the PHV is mirrored.
  \item \textbf{Packet Generator.} A packet generator may generate packets based
  on a specified trigger. A common use case for this feature is periodic packet
  generation based on timers.
\end{compactenum}

\paragraph{Control plane}
RMT programs typically rely on a control plane for configuration, management,
and to handle exceptions and other uncommon processing tasks. The control plane
is implemented to execute on a CPU, either on the host or adjacent to the RMT
pipeline itself.



\subsection{Challenges for TCP on RMT}\label{sec:rmt-challenges}


A TCP stack for RMT must achieve fine-grained parallelization of the transport
logic to provide the segment processing rates necessary for line rate
performance. In particular, doing so comprises the following challenges:


\begin{compactenum}[1.]
  \item \textbf{Unidirectional lock-step pipeline:} The RMT architecture
  utilizes a lock-step pipeline, where each stage operates independently with
  limited local memory and timing. As a consequence, TCP state and logic must
  be partitioned across stages. This introduces \textit{forward} read
  dependencies, where a current stage depends on state in future pipeline
  stages, and \textit{circular} write dependencies that require state updates
  in prior stages. 





  \item \textbf{Limited mirroring:} Mirroring may be employed
  to loop state back into the pipeline, but it must be used
  sparingly to preserve performance, and can take several hundred
  nanoseconds to execute.
\item \textbf{Consistency:} Several segments can concurrently process in
  separate pipeline stages. All segments must observe a consistent and
  up-to-date state snapshot, even for intervening segments while state is
  looped back to resolve circular dependencies.
  \item \textbf{No buffering:} Limited capacity prevents
  prolonged segment buffering within the pipeline, particularly with
  increasing bandwidth-delay products of terabit networks. Buffering is
  also undesirable, as it delays segment delivery.
\end{compactenum}

\noindent
To understand the challenges in-depth, we analyze TAS~\cite{tas}, a
state-of-the-art data center kernel-bypass TCP stack.
TAS already streamlines the TCP transport logic to minimize overhead, providing
an advanced baseline.We particularly focus on TAS' per-connection data-path logic and its state
dependencies. Stateless and read-only logic is easily parallelized, while
off-path logic does not benefit from acceleration.









\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/tcp-state.pdf}
  \caption{TAS TCP connection state and dependencies.}\label{fig:tcp-state}
\end{figure}





Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-state} categorizes TAS' per-connection state into three
groups (cf. RFC 9293~\cite{rfc9293}, Section 3.3.1), each corresponding to
essential TCP data-path functions: reassembly, retransmission, and rate
limiting and flow control, with arrows depicting dependencies among variables:
solid arrows indicte forward dependencies, whereas dotted arrows depict
circular dependencies. We omit congestion control, which TAS implements
out-of-band.
TCP is a bidirectional protocol, with each segment containing both receive and
transmit updates, resulting in intricate dependencies between reassembly and
retransmission state.
We now describe the three groups in more detail.




\paragraph{Reassembly}
TCP is a stream-oriented protocol, but data can arrive in fragments and
out-of-order (OOO), requiring the receiver to buffer these segments to
reassemble the data stream before passing it to the application. TAS defines
the receive window, which represents the receiver's buffer capacity for
incoming data, using two variables: \texttt{rx-next-seq}, the next expected
in-order TCP sequence number, and \texttt{rx-avail}, the number of available
bytes currently within the receive buffer. TAS tracks a single OOO interval
within the receive window, bounded by \texttt{rx-ooo-head} and
\texttt{rx-ooo-tail}. Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-state} shows the complex cyclic
dependencies within the reassembly state (cf. RFC 9293~\cite{rfc9293} Section
3.4). For instance, advancing \texttt{rx-next-seq} upon segment arrival
involves determining whether the segment fits into the receive window
(\texttt{rx-avail}) and whether it merges with an existing OOO interval
(\verb+rx-ooo-*+). Critically, the subsequent update to \texttt{rx\-next-seq}
itself determines the changes to the window and the OOO interval, thus tightly
intertwining all reassembly state.


\paragraph{(Re-)transmission}
TCP stacks detect lost segments by tracking acknowledgments and recover
segments via retransmission, requiring segments to be buffered until they are
acknowledged.
The transmit window is defined by \texttt{tx\-next-ack}, the first
unacknowledged TCP sequence number, \texttt{tx-avail}, the bytes ready for
transmission in the window, and \texttt{tx-sent}, transmitted but
unacknowledged bytes. Additionally, \texttt{tx\-dupack-cnt} counts duplicate
ACKs for fast retransmission. TAS implements go-back-N
retransmission~\cite{tas}, which does not require additional state.
Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-state} shows the dependencies among (re-)transmission
state. ACKs usually fall before \texttt{tx-next-ack} + \texttt{tx-sent}.
However, retransmissions reset \texttt{tx-sent}, allowing valid ACKs to exceed
it, but not \texttt{tx-avail}. This creates a forward dependency between
\texttt{tx-next-ack}, \texttt{tx-avail}, and \texttt{tx-sent} for ACK
validation and transmit window advancement (cf. RFC 9293,
3.10.7.4~\cite{rfc9293}). 

\begin{figure*}[!ht]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/highlevel-arch.pdf}
  \caption{\sys{} overview. The RMT TCP transport logic in \CircledText{6} is
    our focus (\shortsecref{sec:lock-free-sync}).}\label{fig:highlevel-arch}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Rate limiting \& Flow control}
Flow control prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver's
capacity to buffer received segments. Congestion control mitigates network
congestion by rate limiting senders based on network capacity. Both mechanisms
can require senders to buffer ready-to-transmit segments.
\texttt{tx-remote-avail} tracks the remote receive window, advertised by the
remote peer in the TCP segment header, guiding the stack to limit the in-flight
bytes (\texttt{tx-sent}) accordingly. Updating \texttt{tx-remote-avail} solely
for in-order segments introduces dependencies on the reassembly state.
Likewise, halving \texttt{tx-rate} under fast retransmission introduces
dependencies on
(re-)transmission state.





 \section{\sys{} Overview}\label{sec:design}

\sys{} is, to our knowledge, the first TCP stack designed for line-rate TCP
segment processing. \sys{} is general-purpose---it scales to thousands of connections, is robust against packet loss and
congestion, and maintains TCP endpoint compatibility.
Like many other proposals~\cite{flextoe,tas}, \sys{} accelerates TCP processing
for established connections---the common case for high-performance
applications. To do so, it divides the TCP stack into three key components
(Figure~\ref{fig:highlevel-arch}): control plane, application interface, and
accelerated RMT data-path.

\paragraph{Control plane}
The control plane oversees connection lifecycle operations, including
establishment and teardown, and configures the data-path resources and
interfaces. It also handles the congestion control policy and manages other
uncommon scenarios, such as timeouts. It may run either on the host or on a
control CPU alongside the RMT pipeline.

\paragraph{Application interface}
The application interface is provided by the \libsys{} dynamically linkable
library. For compatibility with unmodified applications, \libsys{} supports
POSIX socket API calls. Additionally, it provides a zero-copy API (\libsyszc{})
that allows data-intensive applications to interact directly with \libsys{}
receive and transmit buffers. \libsys{} and the RMT data-path communicate using
DMA.
Each \libsys{} instance (\textit{context}) operates an independent,
flow-controlled DMA channel. 



\paragraph{RMT data-path}
The RMT data-path executes core TCP transport logic for established connections
to ensure reliable and ordered delivery of byte streams directly to/from
\libsys{}. To do so, ingress pipeline stage \CircledText{1} first classifies a
segment into one of three workflows, based on its origin and header:


\smallskip
\begin{compactenum}[1.]
  \item \textbf{RX} processes segments received from the MAC, performing
  reassembly and delivering the payload into \libsys{}’s per-connection receive
  buffers via DMA. \item \textbf{TX} processes DMA transmit notifications from \libsys{} and
  prepares segments for transmission from host transmit buffers under congestion
  and flow control limits.
  \item \textbf{SYNC} periodically updates data-path RX and TX buffer and window availability, triggered from multiple sources.
\end{compactenum}
\smallskip

\noindent
In \CircledText{2}, \sys{} determines the connection and context identifiers for
the pipeline. The lookup uses the segment’s 5-tuple on
RX, or DMA header fields for TX and SYNC. In \CircledText{3}, the TCP sequence
number is translated to a host virtual address for RX segments, and vice versa
for TX packets (\shortsecref{sec:address-translation}). In \CircledText{4},
\sys{} preemptively prepares the segment for its destination, by preparing DMA
headers for RX \& SYNC, and IP\&TCP headers for TX. After this, the pipeline
performs L2/L3 forwarding for TX and non-\sys{} packets \CircledText{5},
and submits the segments to the traffic manager (TM) for egress processing.


The egress pipeline realizes the core TCP transport logic
(\shortsecref{sec:lock-free-sync}), including reassembly
(\shortsecref{sec:reassembly}) and (re-)transmission
(\shortsecref{sec:loss-detection}) \CircledText{6}. It updates the DMA state as
needed for issuing DMA operations (\shortsecref{sec:impl}) \CircledText{7} and
finalizes segment headers before transmission \CircledText{8}. For RX, a DMA
engine transfers the payload to host memory and notifies the application. If an
acknowledgment is needed, the pipeline mirrors the segment to the source
channel for processing and transmission (\shortsecref{sec:ack-generation}).
Leveraging lossless transmission in the egress pipeline, we design the ingress
pipeline for read-only operation and maintain mutable state in the egress
pipeline. This ensures that \sys{} is \textit{drop resistant}. Any packets
dropped in the TM are equivalent to network losses and handled TCP's
retransmission logic.





\section{RMT TCP Transport Logic Design}\label{sec:lock-free-sync}



The heart of \sys{} is its RMT TCP transport logic.\ \sys{} rearchitects TAS'
per-connection logic (Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-state}) to maximize RMT pipeline
parallelism in the common case. To overcome the challenges of
\shortsecref{sec:rmt-challenges}, we adopt these design principles:

\begin{compactenum}[1.]


  \item \textbf{Bump-in-the-wire processing:} To preserve RMT pipeline
  processing bandwidth and to achieve near-hardware latency and throughput,
  \sys{} processes each TCP segment no more than once in the pipeline. Segments
  are never buffered in the pipeline, making judicious use of the limited
  pipeline memory capacity.


  \item \textbf{Optimistic segment processing:} \sys{} optimizes handling
  forward read dependencies with \textit{optimistic processing}, assuming the
  \textit{common case}---in-order segment receipt and delivery---and verifying
  the assumption later, potentially restoring critical state via cyclic updates.

  \item \textbf{Pseudo segment cyclic update:} To resolve cyclic write
  dependencies without disrupting the pipeline, \sys{} injects
  \emph{pseudo segments} into the RMT pipeline via mirroring. These segments are processed
  like regular TCP segments, but are carefully crafted to cause the desired
  state updates in earlier stages without side effects. TCP state is
  always kept consistent, even if such updates may, in exceptional cases,
  briefly reduce pipeline performance.







\end{compactenum}

\noindent
We now detail how \sys{} realizes TCP transport logic in RMT.
First, we describe segment reassembly (\shortsecref{sec:reassembly}), including
how we handle in-order, out-of-window, and out-of-order segments efficiently.
Next, we present the mechanisms for (re-)transmission
(\shortsecref{sec:loss-detection}), emphasizing congestion control and
acknowledgment processing. Finally, we illustrate how \sys{} translates between
TCP sequence numbers and host memory addresses
(\shortsecref{sec:address-translation}), efficiently supporting buffer
management.

\subsection{Segment Reassembly}\label{sec:reassembly}

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/tcp-reassembly.pdf}

  \caption{RMT TCP segment reassembly paths.}\label{fig:tcp-reassembly-algo}
\end{figure}

On RX, segment reassembly involves incorporating any relevant part of a
received segment within the receive window. It requires several computational
steps, including identifying which bytes of the segment are within window,
trimming out-of-window bytes, advancing the window, notifying \libsys{}, and
acknowledging successfully received bytes to the sender. For robustness, \sys{}
tracks and buffers segments of up to one out-of-order (OOO) interval. This
process introduces the complex state dependencies shown in
Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-state} that existing TCP stacks process atomically for each
connection. We now describe how \sys{} realizes reassembly
in sequential pipeline stages, as illustrated in
Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-reassembly-algo}, starting with the common case: in-order
segment reception.













\subsubsection{In-order} \sys{} initially assumes segments arrive in order. It consequently updates
\texttt{rx-next-seq} optimistically for the
\textit{in-order} portion of a segment \CircledText{1} , deferring the \textit{out-of-window}
(OOW) check. Fully duplicate segments, where the entire segment's data sequences
before \texttt{rx-next-seq}, are dropped, while partially duplicate segments
are trimmed. A snapshot of \texttt{rx-next-seq} is forwarded to subsequent
stages along with the (trimmed) segment. Subsequent stages handle in-order and
out-of-order segments differently. We follow the in-order path (top in
Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-reassembly-algo}). In \CircledText{2}, \texttt{rx-avail} is
optimistically decremented based on the trimmed in-order segment. This update
must happen, even for segments that are fully or partially
out-of-window, to maintain consistency with the already updated
\texttt{rx-next-seq}. \CircledText{2} now conducts the OOW check. If the segment
is OOW, \sys{} processes it in the control plane (\shortsecref{sec:oow}).
If an OOO interval is tracked, then \CircledText{3} and \CircledText{4}
decrement \texttt{rx-ooo-head} and \texttt{rx-ooo-tail}, respectively, as they
are represented as offsets from \texttt{rx-next-seq}.
This design guarantees that all segments operate on consistent state. 

\subsubsection{Out-of-window}\label{sec:oow}
A challenging scenario arises for segments that are \textit{in-order} and
(partially) \textit{out-of-window}. For such segments, we have already advanced
the receive window. In this situation, \sys{} must \begin{enumerate*}[label={(\alph*)}]
  \item roll back the state, and
  \item provide consistency for any intervening segments \end{enumerate*}.


Well-behaved TCP stacks will not exceed the advertised flow control window,
making this scenario rare. \sys{} leverages the control plane to resolve it.
When the exceptional \textit{out-of-window} scenario is first detected, the
segment is dropped and the control plane is notified to reset the TCP state to
the value prior to the dropped segment. Meanwhile, any intervening segments
will present as \textit{out-of-window} via a zero \texttt{rx-avail} and are
also dropped, generating acknowledgments advertising a window size of 0 to
pause further transmissions.



\subsubsection{Out-of-order (OOO)}
The OOO path (bottom in Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-reassembly-algo}) concerns only
stages \CircledText{3} and \CircledText{4}---the other stages do nothing.
Leveraging our \textit{bump-in-the-wire} design principle, OOO segments are
directly placed at their position in the per-connection receive payload buffer.
If no OOO interval is currently being tracked, it is set to the segment's
boundaries. Otherwise, the segment merges with the interval's boundaries,
extending \texttt{rx-ooo-tail} \CircledText{3} and \texttt{rx-ooo-head}
\CircledText{4}, respectively, if they overlap with the segment's boundaries.
Non-overlapping OOO segments are dropped.

\subsubsection{Acknowledgment}\label{sec:ack-generation}
For each received TCP segment containing payload, \sys{} generates a pseudo
segment carrying snapshots of the reassembly state (\CircledText{6} in
Figure~\ref{fig:highlevel-arch}). This pseudo segment is mirrored and then
turned into a TCP acknowledgment (\CircledText{8} in
Figure~\ref{fig:highlevel-arch}).
If the pipeline drops the pseudo segment, the effect is identical to network
packet loss of a TCP acknowledgment.


\subsubsection{OOO interval merge}
A cyclic dependency arises when a segment closes the receive window gap to a
tracked OOO interval, as it necessitates advancing \texttt{rx-next-seq} to the
end of the OOO interval and decrementing \texttt{rx-avail} by the same amount.
To resolve the dependency, \sys{} adopts a two-step merge process: after an
in-order segment closes the gap (\texttt{rx-ooo-head} becomes 0) in
\CircledText{4}, \sys{} injects a \emph{pseudo segment} into the pipeline
(combined with any acknowledgment pseudo segment) that has no payload but
covers the entire range between \texttt{rx-next-seq} and \texttt{rx-ooo-tail}. Pseudo segments allow in-order segment reassembly to proceed normally, even
when the OOO interval is temporarily unmerged. If pseudo segments are dropped,
the OOO interval will stay unmerged, causing further incoming segments to
generate further pseudo segments. Until the merge completes, \sys{}'s ability
to handle out-of-order packets is diminished due to the inability to establish
a new OOO interval. However, this scenario is exceedingly rare due to the RMT
pipeline's high segment processing bandwidth.




\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/tcp-loss-detection-tx.pdf}
  \caption{RMT TCP processing for TX workflow.}\label{fig:tcp-loss-detection-tx-algo}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Notification}
Each \textit{in-order} segment that advances the receive window triggers a
notification to \libsys{}, indicating the payload buffer offset up to which
data is ready for application consumption. When a segment closes the gap to an
OOO interval, \libsys{} is notified ahead of the pseudo segment merge.



\subsubsection{Receive window replenishment}
As the reassembled payload fills the receive buffer, it must be replenished
periodically.
\libsys{} triggers the SYNC workflow when the application has consumed more than
a predefined portion of the buffer (default: $\frac{1}{4}$). SYNC
increments \textit{rx-avail} by the amount specified by \libsys{}.


\subsection{(Re-)transmission}\label{sec:loss-detection}


(Re-)transmission processing is considerably simpler and without cyclic
dependencies due to go-back-N retransmission.
After reassembly, SYNC (\shortsecref{sec:scheduling}), TX
(\shortsecref{sec:tx}), and RX (\shortsecref{sec:ack_rx}) all traverse these
paths as TCP is bidirectional due to acknowledgments being piggybacked on
received segments.




\subsubsection{Congestion Control (SYNC)}\label{sec:scheduling}
To remain robust to packet loss and congestion, \sys{} supports
DCTCP~\cite{dctcp} as the default congestion control policy.
Like other TCP stacks~\cite{tas, flextoe,ccp}, \sys{} locates the congestion
control policy in the control plane, which simplifies implementation, making it
easy to add new policies. The data-path gathers per-connection metrics like
acknowledged bytes, ECN-marked bytes, duplicate ACKs, and round-trip times
(RTTs). The control plane periodically processes these metrics to compute a new
transmission rate. Transmission credits based on the rate are conveyed to the
data-path and \libsys{} via periodic SYNCs, updating \texttt{tx-credits} and
potentially \texttt{tx-next-ack}. Upon SYNC, \libsys{} can reclaim buffer space
for acknowledged data and initiate new transmissions. SYNC may also be
initiated upon a retransmission timeout. In such cases, SYNC signals \libsys{}
to reset its transmission head and initiate retransmissions. To conserve
pipeline bandwidth, \sys{} pauses SYNC workflows for inactive connections (no
data transmission for $N$ RTTs). For uncongested flows with short messages that
underutilize credits, the control plane reduces SYNC frequency. \libsys{}
self-paces SYNCs, triggering them only as the transmit window nears exhaustion.

\subsubsection{Transmission (TX)}\label{sec:tx}

When sufficient credits are available, \libsys{} \textit{pushes} any new data
into the data-path (Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-loss-detection-tx-algo}). This approach
minimizes latency and data-path complexity, leveraging \sys's
\textit{bump-in-the-wire} design principle. \sys{} determines TCP sequence
numbers based on the DMA offset within the host transmit buffer. Any segments
with sequence numbers below \texttt{tx-next-ack} (e.g., due to stale
retransmissions that have since been ACK'ed to the data-path) are dropped
\CircledText{1}. If the segment extends beyond the current transmit window,
\texttt{tx-avail} is updated to reflect it \CircledText{3}. Transmission is
credit limited (cf.~\shortsecref{sec:scheduling}) and flow controlled in
\CircledText{4}---the segment size is deducted from \texttt{tx-credits} and the
segment is dropped when \texttt{tx-credits} is zero or when the number of
unacknowledged bytes exceeds the flow control window \texttt{tx-remote-avail}
\CircledText{5}.

\subsubsection{Acknowledgment Processing (RX)}\label{sec:ack_rx}
\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/tcp-loss-detection-ack.pdf}
  \caption{RMT TCP processing path for RX workflow.}\label{fig:tcp-loss-detection-ack-algo}
\end{figure}

For any received ACK, \sys{} optimistically updates \texttt{tx-next-ack} in
\CircledText{1}, discarding any duplicates
(Figure~\ref{fig:tcp-loss-detection-ack-algo}). Similar to reassembly, \sys{}
is unable to check whether an acknowledgment is \textit{out-of-window} at this
stage. In \CircledText{2}, \texttt{tx-dupack-cnt} increments for duplicate ACKs
and resets otherwise. Upon receiving 3 duplicate ACKs, \sys{} triggers fast
retransmission and notifies \libsys{} of the latest \texttt{tx-next-ack} via
DMA. The \textit{out-of-window} check occurs in stage \CircledText{3} when
updating \texttt{tx-avail}. A well-behaved TCP stack should never send
acknowledgments for untransmitted data. If it does, \sys{} notifies the control
plane to reset the connection. Upon fast retransmission, \texttt{tx-credits} is
halved in \CircledText{4}, similar to TCP Reno. ACKs that are in-order as
determined by the reassembly state snapshots (\shortsecref{sec:reassembly}),
update \texttt{tx-remote-avail}, the remote peer's receive window status, in
\CircledText{5}.











\subsection{Sequence-Address Translation}\label{sec:address-translation}
\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/address-translation.pdf}
  \caption{Sequence-address translation with double buffer.}\label{fig:address-translation}
\end{figure}

\sys{}'s per-connection payload buffers adopt double buffering, where the
entire buffer is mapped twice consecutively in \libsys{} virtual address space
(Figure~\ref{fig:address-translation}). This design efficiently handles wrap
around at the buffer boundary, eliminating the need to split a DMA operation
into two separate transfers. The pipeline translates addresses by adding the
connection's payload buffer base address to an offset derived from the segment's
TCP sequence number and vice versa.




 \section{Implementation}\label{sec:impl}
\sys{}’s data-path is implemented on an Intel Tofino2-based switch,
a commercially available RMT pipeline architecture. For DMA, we utilize RDMA.
\sys{} is implemented in 20,775 lines of code (LoC). The P4 code for the
offloaded data-path has 2,597 LoC. The control-plane is split into two
components: one on the host and another, \texttt{SwitchConf}, on the switch CPU.
The host control-plane interacts with \texttt{SwitchConf} to configure switch
data-path resources such as match-action tables. Moreover, \texttt{SwitchConf}
runs the congestion control policy and processes all control plane
notifications. \texttt{SwitchConf} interacts with the data-path via Intel’s
proprietary bfrt C++ API. They are implemented in 3,352 and 6,917 C++ LoC
respectively. \libsys{} is implemented in 7,909 C++ LoC, utilizing
\texttt{libibverbs} to interact with the RDMA NIC without kernel intervention.
Our prototype leverages some RDMA and Tofino2 features for optimizations,
described below.

\paragraph{DMA}
\libsys{} interacts with the data-path via the RDMA verbs API. During
initialization, it establishes an unreliable connection (UC) RDMA queue pair
per context with the data-path. Typically, each application thread uses a
separate context, akin to per-core NIC queues in traditional network stacks.
Connections owned by a context are multiplexed onto a single queue pair,
avoiding RDMA NIC connection scalability bottlenecks. Both \libsys{} and the
data-path use RDMA writes (with immediate for notifications) to transmit or
receive data from host payload buffers. \libsys{} allocates per-connection
payload buffers and registers them with the RDMA NIC, storing the buffer's
virtual address and remote memory key in the data-path.
The egress pipeline assigns an RDMA sequence number to each packet. To ensure
lossless RDMA operation, PFC is enabled between the host and the switch.


\paragraph{Interrupt-driven operation}
By default, \libsys{} operates in polling mode, constantly querying the
completion queue for events. However, after 10ms of inactivity, \libsys{}
switches to interrupt-mode by leveraging RDMA completion event channels
(\texttt{ibv\_comp\_channel}), enabling the application to sleep when waiting
for IO.












\paragraph{Limitations}
Tofino2’s checksum engine does not support computing or validating payload
checksums, preventing our implementation from handling TCP and RDMA iCRC
checksums. However, TCP and RDMA hardware checksum units are common and adding
support would be straightforward.

 \section{Evaluation}\label{sec:eval}
We evaluate \sys{} by addressing the following questions:
\begin{compactenum}[\labelitemi]
  \item \textbf{Performance:} Does \sys{} deliver predictable $\mu$s-scale
  latency and high message rate for latency-sensitive RPC workloads
  (\shortsecref{sec:rpc-eval})? Can \sys{} sustain terabit-scale throughput
  with near-zero CPU utilization (\shortsecref{sec:stream-eval})? Can it scale
  efficiently to support a large number of applications and connections
  (\shortsecref{sec:rpc-eval})?
  \item \textbf{Efficiency:} Does \sys{} achieve better performance-per-watt
  compared to host-based stacks? How does it compare to ASIC and FPGA-based
  offloaded stacks (\shortsecref{sec:power-efficiency})?
  \item \textbf{Flexibility:} What is \sys{}'s RMT-pipeline resource utilization
  and does it leave sufficient room for flexibly implementing additional
  data center networking features (\shortsecref{sec:rmt-resource-usage})?
  \item \textbf{Robustness:} Is \sys{} resilient to packet loss and
  congestion? Can \sys{} ensure performance isolation with co-located latency-sensitive
  and bandwidth-intensive applications?
  (\shortsecref{sec:robustness-eval})
\end{compactenum}

\paragraph{Testbed}
Our evaluation cluster comprises six Intel Xeon Gold 6430 machines, each with
32-core (64 hyperthreads) running at 2GHz, 256GB RAM, and 126.5MB aggregate
cache. Each machine is equipped with a RDMA-capable 200G Mellanox ConnectX-6
NIC, all connected to an 32$\times$400G Intel Tofino-2 based Netberg Aurora 810
switch. We configure the NICs in 100G mode as our switch fails to negotiate our
NICs into 200G speeds. Two machines are designated as servers, with Priority
Flow Control (PFC) enabled for lossless RDMA, while the remaining machines
function as clients. To ensure high performance and low latency, we disable
turbo boost and set frequency scaling to performance mode. Power measurements
are obtained via the IPMI interface of both the machines and the switch.

\paragraph{Baselines}
We compare \sys{} performance against the Linux TCP stack, the TAS
kernel-bypass TCP stack, and RDMA\@. Unless otherwise specified, clients use
the TAS network stack to generate network traffic. TAS struggles with large
flows due to high payload copy overheads, failing to saturate the 100G line
rate with a single connection. To mitigate this bottleneck in such client
workloads, we elide payload copying in TAS and transmit junk data instead
(TAS-nocopy). We use identical application binaries that use sockets-based
\texttt{epoll()} interface across all baselines, except for RDMA\@. For the
RDMA baseline, we adapt our benchmarks to use the \texttt{libibverbs}
interface. We use DCTCP as the default congestion control policy. 

\subsection{Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs)}\label{sec:rpc-eval}
RPC workloads simultaneously demand low latency, high packet processing rates,
and scalability to numerous applications and connections, imposing a
significant overhead on host TCP stacks.\ \sys{}'s bump-in-the-wire design
achieves low, constant TCP processing latency even at throughput beyond several
million segments per second, and high efficiency by offloading TCP processing
entirely from CPUs. We demonstrate that \sys{} excels at this workload using an
echo server benchmark.

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{plots/rpcecho_unloadedlatency.pdf}
  \caption{Unloaded RPC round-trip time (RTT).}\label{fig:rpc-unloaded-latency}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Unloaded latency} Figure~\ref{fig:rpc-unloaded-latency} compares the round-trip time (RTT)
distribution of different network stacks for a single connection with one
in-flight request, evaluated for two message sizes: 64B and 1024B. We note that
our setup bypasses egress processing for non-\sys{} packets, reducing RTTs for
baselines---a conventional switch data-path would require both ingress and
egress processing for all packets. Our measurements further overestimate
\sys{}’s true latency as we handle \sys{}-\sys{} connections via recirculation,
inflating \sys{}'s latency relative to RDMA\@. Eliminating recirculation would reduce latency to within $< 1\mu s$ of RDMA\@.

\sys{}’s bump-in-the-wire design achieves low and predictable latencies,
outperforming TAS by as much as $4.3\times$ at the tail, and Linux
by $5\times$ at the median and $25.6\times$ at the tail. Unlike the
RMT-pipeline, CPUs fail to exploit the inherent parallelism in network
processing, and their sequential execution causes high latency.
Additionally, CPU-based stacks exhibit higher latencies
for larger message sizes due to the overhead of copying the payload to/from
network buffers. Supporting the sockets interface in \sys{} requires an
additional copy from \libsys{}’s per-connection payload buffers to
user-supplied buffers, introducing a small latency overhead, negligible for
small RPCs. The \libsyszc{} zerocopy interface eliminates this overhead and
incurs only a $2\mu s$ higher latency than RDMA\@.

  \caption{Load-latency across network stacks (note different x \& y axis ranges).}\label{fig:rpc-load-latency}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Throughput-latency curves}
Does \sys{} provide a high RPC rate while maintaining low tail latency? Figure
~\ref{fig:rpc-load-latency} presents the latency profile of an echo server
across stacks. To increase load, the benchmark uses up to 32 server cores and
scales the number of connections using multiple clients, each leaving a single
64B RPC in-flight.

\sys{} performance closely matches RDMA\@. It achieves $32.5$ MOps/sec with a
$14\mu s$/$24\mu s$ median/tail latency. This surpasses TAS throughput by
$1.3 \times$ at $5 \times$ lower latency. However, \sys{}’s peak throughput
falls short of RDMA due to \sys{}-\sys{} connections requiring recirculation.
At $32.5$ MOps/sec, the RMT-pipeline processes $4\times$ the packet rate ($=130$
M pkt/sec), as each message involves processing requests, responses, and their
corresponding ACKs, saturating the 100G recirculation bandwidth. To bypass this
bottleneck, we use a \sys{}-TAS configuration, with a \sys{} server and TAS
clients. In this setup, \sys{} achieves a peak throughput of $40$ MOps/sec
($1.67\times$ TAS), matching RDMA, at a slightly higher latency due to
client-side TAS overheads. Nearing $40$ MOps/sec, both \sys{} and RDMA
experience tail latency spikes as they approach the NIC’s processing capacity.
Linux is inefficient, delivering $10\times$ lower throughput and
$78\times$ higher latency compared to \sys{}.

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{plots/rpc_core_scalability.pdf}
  \caption{Core scalability.}\label{fig:rpc-core-scalability}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Core scalability}
To evaluate core scalability, we repeat the previous experiment varying server
cores, sweeping connections for each configuration to find the optimal
operating point (knee of the throughput-latency curve). In this benchmark,
\sys{} is tested with TAS clients.
Figure~\ref{fig:rpc-core-scalability} demonstrates that \sys{} is highly
scalable, with data-path performance invariant to the number of contexts.
\sys{} multiplexes TCP connections onto per-core DMA channels
(\textit{contexts}), avoiding RDMA’s scalability limits, steering payload
directly to application cores (akin to aRFS~\cite{aRFS}).\ \sys{}’s performance
peaks with 8 cores, reaching the NIC bottleneck. At this point, \sys{}
surpasses TAS’s peak throughput, while maintaining 4.3$\times$ lower tail
latency. Linux performance remains poor.

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{plots/rpc_conn_scalability.pdf}
  \caption{Connection scalability.}\label{fig:rpc-conn-scalability}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Connection scalability}
Figure~\ref{fig:rpc-conn-scalability} shows \sys{}’s connection scalability,
using 24 server cores.\ \sys{} saturates the NIC throughput at 768 connections,
achieving $1.8\times$ and $10\times$ higher throughput than TAS and Linux,
respectively. Beyond this point, further connections yield no gain, and
throughput slightly drops due to increased tail latency as NIC capacity
saturates.
Existing TCP stacks scale poorly with connections, suffering from cache misses
due to large per-connection state and cache pollution due to interference with
application state. Even RDMA and NPU-based offloads struggle with scalability
due to limited on-NIC fast memory~\cite{erpc,flextoe}. In contrast, \sys{}’s
data-path is designed to handle 32k connections without performance degradation
as the connection count increases, as each stage accesses local memory with
constant access latency. Higher connection counts can be supported by sharding
TCP state tables across stages (\shortsecref{sec:rmt-resource-usage}).

\subsection{Byte Streaming}\label{sec:stream-eval}

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{plots/stream_rx_singleflow_pps.pdf}
  \caption{Streaming performance with different segment sizes.}\label{fig:stream-bandwidth}
\end{figure}

Streaming bandwidth is critical for modern storage and AI workloads.
CPU-based stacks like Linux and TAS fail to saturate line rate on a single
core, even with hardware-assisted payload copy
optimizations~\cite{cai2021understanding,flextoe}. Critically, accelerating
copies with specialized DMA engines~\cite{zeronic} doesn't resolve this, as
single-core protocol processing becomes the bottleneck limiting terabit
scalability (\shortsecref{sec:arch-survey}). Consequently, hardware-offloaded
transports like RDMA and Chelsio TOE, despite their inflexibility, are
increasingly preferred for streaming.


Can \sys{} match RDMA’s performance? In this benchmark, a TAS-nocopy client
transmits packets in an open-loop (similar to iperf~\cite{iperf}) to a single
server core that discards incoming payloads. To provide different intensities
of protocol to payload processing, the benchmark varies the segment size by
adjusting the maximum transmission unit (MTU).
To avoid payload copying in the sockets layer, we use the \libsyszc{}
interface, comparing against the equivalent low-level TAS interface (TAS-ll),
though TAS still requires copying the payload between network buffers and
application memory.

Figure~\ref{fig:stream-bandwidth} shows that \sys{} matches RDMA's single-core
packet rate of \textasciitilde{}25M pkts/sec, independent of packet size,
reaching line rate for higher MTUs. At 8K MTU, \sys{}'s potential single-core
throughput exceeds 1.6 Tbps ($= 25M * 8 * 8K = 1600G$). The bottleneck remains
NIC and CPU processing~\cite{kalia2016design}, as the RMT pipeline's processing
capacity is far greater (6B pkts/sec for Tofino2~\cite{netberg_aurora810}).
TAS performance is limited to \textasciitilde{}5M pkts/sec per core, that drops
for packets $>$512B due to copy overhead. Crucially, even with hardware copy
offload, TAS's single-core protocol processing prevents terabit scalability.
This bottleneck is also present in NPU-based stacks like
FlexTOE~\cite{flextoe}. Linux, again, performs poorly.

\subsection{Power Efficiency}\label{sec:power-efficiency}
We evaluate the power consumption of different network stacks using
FlexKVS~\cite{flexnic}, a scalable, high-performance key-value store, inspired
by memcached. Key-value store workloads rely heavily on short RPCs, where the
TCP stack can consume up to 48\% of per-request CPU cycles~\cite{flextoe}.The experiment uses a workload of 1M uniformly distributed key-value pairs (8B
keys, 64B values, $0.99$ GET:SET ratio). We first record baseline power for the
server (including NIC) and switch. Then, the workload runs for 2 minutes while
measuring total power consumption and application performance. This process is
repeated varying server threads and connections, with each connection limited
to a single in-flight request.


\begin{figure}[t!]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{plots/flexkvs_experiment.pdf}
  \caption{Throughput-per-watt and tail latency for FlexKVS key-value store workload.}\label{fig:flexkvs-power}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:flexkvs-power}, plotting throughput-per-watt and tail latency
across server configurations (\# threads, \# connections), demonstrates
\sys{}'s performance-per-watt advantage over host stacks. Even \sys{}'s worst
case exceeds TAS's best by 1.2$\times$ in throughput-per-watt with 5$\times$
lower 99.99p tail latency; \sys{}'s best configuration achieves 2$\times$ TAS
throughput-per-watt and exceeds TAS's best tail latency. Linux performs at
least an order of magnitude worse than \sys{} in throughput-per-watt while
suffering from two orders of magnitude higher latency.
Importantly, the switch's power consumption varies by no more than 4W between
baselines and \sys{}, with the majority of power savings stemming from reduced
host CPU usage. Additionally, RMT-pipeline-based switches consume power
comparable to non-programmable commodity switches of similar aggregate
bandwidth~\cite{agrawal2020intel,metamorphosis}, while FPGAs are power
hungry~\cite{amdalveou200}. We expect an RDMA-based implementation of FlexKVS
to yield results equivalent to \sys{}, with significant gains over FPGA stacks.

\subsection{Flexibility}\label{sec:rmt-resource-usage}

Unlike inflexible hardware transports, \sys{} provides flexibility via
high-level P4 programmability. Table~\ref{tab:tofino-resource-usage} shows
\sys{}'s RMT-pipeline resource consumption. Despite offloading complex TCP
protocol processing, our resource consumption remains modest, using
approximately 30\% of the memory and compute resources to support 32,768
connections and 1,024 contexts.\ \sys{}'s data-path processes 3.2 Tbps ($8
\times 400$G) line-rate at a total processing latency (excluding queuing
delays) of 395ns and a power consumption of 2.81W for the RMT pipeline
(excluding SerDes, MAC, TM). Our implementation already includes basic
L2/L3-routing for non-\sys{} packets, but low resource consumption leaves ample
headroom for new functions in the data-path. We demonstrate this flexibility by
accelerating a shared log application~\cite{corfu} and implementing transport
extensions (Timely congestion control, delayed ACKs).



\paragraph{Shared log}
Critical data center applications, including databases~\cite{delos}, replicated
state machines~\cite{scalog}, and storage clusters~\cite{corfu}, rely on a
shared log abstraction. Shared logs allow multiple clients to linearize state
updates~\cite{luo2024lazylog,corfu}.

Inspired by NoPaxos~\cite{nopaxos}, we accelerate a shared log microbenchmark
with a tailored \sys{} API\@: after the application registers its shared log
buffer address and client connections with the data-path, \sys{} sequences
incoming log records across connections and directly deposits them into the
shared log buffer using a buffer tail pointer within the
data-path~\footnote{Clients ensure log records are not fragmented across TCP
segments.}. Our design guarantees that records from the same connection are
appended to the shared log in order, resulting in a linearized shared log. If
out-of-order segments arrive, \sys{} reserves space up to the highest sequence
number, creating gaps; the application later fills these gaps using the
corresponding segments, which are redirected to it by \sys{}. Our
implementation required an additional 156 P4 LoC and increased power
consumption by 0.29W.

Evaluating this approach with a shared log benchmark (up to 32 clients,
64--1024B variable sized records, up to 256 in-flight records per client),
\sys{} saturates line-rate using only a single core. In contrast, TAS requires
up to 5 CPU cores (3 TAS + 2 application) for the same task. \sys{}'s
efficiency stems from eliminating sequencing, protocol processing, and payload
copying from the CPU in the common case (no packet loss). Achieving similar
acceleration with RDMA is challenging, especially for variable-sized records,
due to requiring multiple round-trips for sequencing and writing each
record~\cite{kalia2016design}.

\paragraph{Timely}
Congestion control remains an evolving research area, with numerous policies
developed to address diverse network conditions and performance
objectives~\cite{1rma}. Timely~\cite{timely}, a congestion control policy that
estimates network congestion based on round-trip time (RTT) variations, is a
notable example. To implement Timely, we leverage the hardware timestamping
feature of the Tofino2 architecture to add TCP timestamps to
segments~\cite{rfc7323}. The data-path computes precise per-flow exponentially
weighted RTT moving averages (EWMAs), involving complex arithmetic. We utilize
the low-pass filter (LPF) unit on Tofino2, which can be configured to compute
EWMAs efficiently~\cite{tofino2_ewma}. The policy, implemented in 290 C++ LoC
in the control plane, periodically processes these RTTs to compute a new
transmission rate. The Timely data-path implementation requires 64 P4 LoC,
$\leq$5\% additional data-path resources, and 0.37W extra MAU power.


\paragraph{Delayed ACKs}
Delayed or cumulative ACKs~\cite{rfc1122} issue one ACK for every $M$
consecutively received segments and significantly reduce sender and network
load~\cite{dctcp}. For example, in RPC workloads, piggybacking the request ACK
onto the response segment can halve the sender's packet processing overhead.
Implementing this feature in the \sys{} data-path requires an additional state
variable to track unacknowledged segments. This counter increments with each
in-order segment and triggers an acknowledgment pseudo-segment only when it
reaches threshold $M$. Transmitted segments or acknowledgments reset the
counter. Out-of-order segments prompt immediate acknowledgments for faster
recovery. The control-plane manages the delayed ACK timer by monitoring this
counter. This required 42 P4 LoC, increased SRAM usage by 3\% and power by
0.05W. We assessed the impact of delayed ACKs by benchmarking echo server with
a \sys{} server and a TAS client utilizing a single fast-path core. TAS load
was gradually increased by increasing connections, each leaving a single RPC in
flight, until peak throughput was observed. Enabling delayed ACKs in \sys{}
improved peak throughput by 24\% by reducing TAS fast-path core load.

\subsection{Robustness}\label{sec:robustness-eval}

\paragraph{Packet drops}
\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{plots/stream_rx_drops.pdf}
  \caption{Streaming goodput under random packet drops.}\label{fig:stream-drops}
\end{figure}

We measure single-connection streaming throughput while randomly discarding
packets with varying probability (Figure~\ref{fig:stream-drops}). This workload
maintains many in-flight packets, ensuring losses trigger OOO processing. Due
to our implementation requiring recirculation for \sys{}-\sys{} connections, we
use a TAS sender for both \sys{} and TAS receiver configurations. This isolates
the evaluation to receiver-side reassembly capabilities; congestion control and
retransmissions are assessed separately (Figure~\ref{fig:incast-response}).

\sys{}’s transport logic closely mirrors TAS, featuring 1-OOO reassembly on
the receiver side and go-back-N retransmission on the sender. Under low packet
loss rates (up to $10^{-4}$), \sys{} achieves up to $1.3\times$ higher
throughput than TAS due to faster acknowledgments accelerating recovery, though
performance is comparable at $0.1\%$ loss. FlexTOE~\cite{flextoe} provides
further comparisons to Linux and the Chelsio TOE\@. Linux withstands higher loss
rates due to its more sophisticated reassembly and recovery mechanisms,
including selective acknowledgments. In contrast, the ASIC-based Chelsio TOE
suffers a steep performance decline even under moderate packet loss rates.
Notably, RDMA drops all out-of-order segments, leading to poor performance under
packet loss~\cite{mittal2018revisiting}. Implementing 1-block SACK in \sys{}
using our 2-step merge design is feasible and is left as future work.

\paragraph{Congestion control}
\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{plots/incast.pdf}
  \caption{Streaming performance under incast.}\label{fig:incast-response}
\end{figure}

To evaluate congestion control, we simulate incast by using a TAS receiver that
implements traffic shaping. The shaper limits ingress bandwidth (corresponding
to the incast degree), uses tail-drop, marks ECN above a queue occupancy
threshold (determined experimentally as 130), and delivers packets to the TAS
logic at a fixed bandwidth. Figure~\ref{fig:incast-response} presents the
results for a single-connection streaming workload under varying congestion
levels, where the black ticks mark the optimal bandwidth achievable.

\sys{} with its control-plane-driven DCTCP and credit-based rate enforcement
effectively regulates transmission, minimizing loss and matching the shaped line
rate. In contrast, \sys{} without congestion control (\sys{}-NoCC) transmits
aggressively, causing excessive tail drops  --- even when traffic shaping
is disabled (incast degree=1) since it significantly outpaces the TAS receiver,
resulting in up to 50$\times$ lower throughput. TAS and Linux also regulate
their rates effectively but fail to achieve maximum possible throughput at low
incast degrees ($\leq$ 2) due to transport stack inefficiencies.

\paragraph{Performance isolation}
Run-to-completion based TCP stacks struggle to isolate the performance of
latency-sensitive (LS) and bandwidth-intensive (BI) applications. Specifically
with TAS, when LS connections share the same TAS fast-path core with BI
connections, packet processing for the LS connections can be blocked behind
packets from BI connections, resulting in inflated tail latency for LS
connections, and reduced bandwidth for BI connections due to high packet rates
from LS\@. This phenomenon is also observed with Linux when the cores are
oversubscribed~\cite{cai2021understanding}.

To evaluate performance isolation, we co-located an echo server RPC workload
with 32 latency-sensitive (LS) connections, each maintaining a single request
in flight, and a streaming workload with 4 bandwidth-intensive (BI)
connections, each transferring data at 5 Gbps. We initially measured the
performance in isolation using both TAS (with a single fast-path core) and
\sys{}, and compare with concurrent execution, provisioning two TAS fast-path
cores to avoid potential bottlenecks. TAS employs a hash function for
connection-to-core assignment, resulting in a mixture of LS and BI flows.

\begin{figure}[t!]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{plots/perf_isolation_colocation.pdf}
  \caption{Performance isolation for Latency-sensitive and Bandwidth-intensive connections.}\label{fig:perf-isolation}
\end{figure}

As depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:perf-isolation}, \sys{} ensures optimal
performance for both LS and BI flows without interference, owing to its
consistent per-packet processing overhead, independent of payload size, and
payload steering directly to corresponding application cores via independent
DMA channels, preventing cache pollution. In contrast, TAS exhibited an 18\%
increase in tail latency for LS flows and a 30\% decrease in bandwidth for BI
flows when co-located.
 \section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Software stack improvements}
To reduce software TCP overhead and improve scalability, significant proposals
have rearchitected stacks via optimized
interfaces~\cite{affinity_accept,fastsocket,mtcp,megapipe,io_uring,io_uring_man,linuxzerocopy,stackmap},
kernel-bypass techniques~\cite{arrakis,ix,mtcp,tas,demikernel}, efficient
drivers~\cite{packetmill,niq,netmap,reframer,258955,ccnic}, hardware
assistance~\cite{aRFS,jumbo,about_nics,tso,ddio,ioat}, and disaggregated
designs~\cite{flextoe,netchannel}.
Yet, scaling to terabit speeds efficiently remains
elusive~\cite{flextoe,cai2021understanding}. A major reason is that CPUs fail
to exploit the inherent parallelism in network processing tasks. Instead,
\sys{} leverages the RMT architecture to enable line-rate TCP processing at
high efficiency.

\paragraph{Co-designed transports}
Tight application-transport
couplings~\cite{erpc,kalia2016fasst,dragojevic2014farm,homa,r2p2,i10,1rma},
burden developers with transport-level complexities, intricate buffer
management, and restrictive execution models, sacrificing generality, and
hindering software reuse.\ \sys{} instead offloads the TCP protocol in a
flexible manner, and remains broadly compatible with existing applications and
deployments.

\paragraph{FPGA stacks}
FPGAs are a highly expressive platform for high-performance
offload~\cite{catapult}. Tonic~\cite{tonic} demonstrates in simulation that
high-performance, flexible TCP offload might be possible. Several
proposals~\cite{beehive,limago,pigasus} add TCP support on an FPGA, but lack
integration with general-purpose applications running on the host.
Dagger~\cite{dagger} co-designs the memory interconnect with an FPGA-offloaded
RPC stack, but does not support TCP\@. ZeroNIC~\cite{zeronic} accelerates
payload copy via FPGA, but TCP protocol processing remains on the CPU\@.
Enso~\cite{enso} designs a streaming NIC driver interface instead of a
packetized interface.\ \sys{} also uses a streaming interface to transfer
payload. While FPGAs enable flexible offload~\cite{accelnet,tonic}, they are
power hungry (e.g., modern solutions use 225W~\cite{amdalveou200}), negating
efficiency benefits of saving host CPUs. Their near-hardware programming model
makes development difficult and slow, relative to agile software
lifecycles~\cite{catapult,kernelinterposeflexible}.\ \sys{} rivals ASIC-level
power efficiency, and retains high development velocity.

\paragraph{SmartNIC stacks}
Leveraging SmartNICs for network virtualization offload is common in data
centers~\cite{amazon_nitro,google_ipu,intel_ipu,catapult}.
AccelTCP~\cite{acceltcp} offloads TCP connection management and
splicing~\cite{tcp_splice} to NPU-SmartNICs, while IO-TCP~\cite{io-tcp}
offloads disk I/O and TCP packet transfer to CPU-SmartNICs, but the TCP
data-path remains on the host. FlexTOE~\cite{flextoe} supports full, flexible
offload to NPU-SmartNICs, but its transport logic scalability is limited by
single-core NPU performance~\cite{chen2024demystifyingdpa,flextoe}.

\paragraph{RMT transport acceleration}
The RMT architecture has emerged as a promising for flexible packet
processing~\cite{pegasus,mind,concordia,redplane}. R2P2~\cite{r2p2} is a
UDP-based RPC stack, that utilizes RMT for load balancing. GEM leverages the
RMT pipeline to implement lightweight RDMA to access external
memory~\cite{gem,tea,ribosome}.\ \sys{} takes inspiration to offload the entire
TCP data-path within RMT\@. Conweave~\cite{conweave} implements network load
balancing utilizing the RMT pipeline to buffer out-of-order RDMA packets under
congestion. LinkGuardian~\cite{linkguardian} implements link-local
retransmission for corrupted packets in RMT\@. Several packet scheduling and
congestion control proposals use RMT~\cite{rmtcalendarq,rmtalloc,rmtfairq,bfc}.
None of them provide transport offload, nor do they obviate the need for an
end-to-end reliable transport protocol like TCP, as provided by \sys{}.
 \section{Conclusion}
\sys{} redefines the design space of high-performance TCP stacks by
demonstrating that full transport-layer functionality can be achieved within the
constraints of the Reconfigurable Match-Action Table (RMT) architecture. By
embracing pipeline-parallelism, optimistic concurrency, and lightweight
pseudo-segment updates, \sys{} delivers terabit-scale throughput, low latency,
and exceptional energy efficiency—matching the performance of specialized
hardware like RDMA, while retaining the flexibility and compatibility of
software-defined networking. Our prototype implementation on an Intel Tofino2
switch confirms that RMT data planes can support stateful, loss-resilient, and
scalable transport protocols, setting a foundation for the next generation of
SmartNICs and data center networks.

title: A derivative-free regularization algorithm for equality constrained nonlinear least squares problems
summary:
In this paper, we study the equality constrained nonlinear least squares
problem, where the Jacobian matrices of the objective function and constraints
are unavailable or expensive to compute. We approximate the Jacobian matrices
via orthogonal spherical smoothing and propose a derivative-free regularization
algorithm for solving the problem. At each iteration, a regularized augmented
Lagrangian subproblem is solved to obtain a Newton-like step. If a sufficient
decrease in the merit function of the approximate KKT system is achieved, the
step is accepted, otherwise a derivative-free LM algorithm is applied to get
another step to satisfy the sufficient decrease condition. It is shown that the
algorithm either finds an approximate KKT point with arbitrary high probability
or converges to a stationary point of constraints violation almost surely.

title: Darboux formulae for linear hyperbolic equations in discrete case
summary:
In the second half of the 19th century Darboux obtained determinant formulae
that provide the general solution for a linear hyperbolic second order PDE with
finite Laplace series. These formulae played an important role in his study of
the theory of surfaces and, in particular, in the theory of conjugate nets.
During the last three decades discrete analogs of conjugate nets (Q-nets) were
actively studied. Laplace series can be defined also for hyperbolic difference
operators. We prove discrete analogs of Darboux formulae for discrete and
semi-discrete hyperbolic operators with finite Laplace series.

title: Optimal Execution in Intraday Energy Markets under Hawkes Processes with Transient Impact
summary:
This paper investigates optimal execution strategies in intraday energy
markets through a mutually exciting Hawkes process model. Calibrated to data
from the German intraday electricity market, the model effectively captures key
empirical features, including intra-session volatility, distinct intraday
market activity patterns, and the Samuelson effect as gate closure approaches.
By integrating a transient price impact model with a bivariate Hawkes process
to model the market order flow, we derive an optimal trading trajectory for
energy companies managing large volumes, accounting for the specific trading
patterns in these markets. A back-testing analysis compares the proposed
strategy against standard benchmarks such as Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP)
and Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP), demonstrating substantial cost
reductions across various hourly trading products in intraday energy markets.

bib.abstract: Market impact is a key concept in the study of financial markets and several models have been proposed in the literature so far. The Transient Impact Model (TIM) posits that the price at high frequency time scales is a linear combination of the signs of the past executed market orders, weighted by a so-called propagator function. An alternative description -- the History Dependent Impact Model (HDIM) -- assumes that the deviation between the realised order sign and its expected level impacts the price linearly and permanently. The two models, however, should be extended since prices are a priori influenced not only by the past order flow, but also by the past realisation of returns themselves. In this paper, we propose a two-event framework, where price-changing and non price-changing events are considered separately. Two-event propagator models provide a remarkable improvement of the description of the market impact, especially for large tick stocks, where the events of price changes are very rare and very informative. Specifically the extended approach captures the excess anti-correlation between past returns and subsequent order flow which is missing in one-event models. Our results document the superior performances of the HDIMs even though only in minor relative terms compared to TIMs. This is somewhat surprising, because HDIMs are well grounded theoretically, while TIMs are, strictly speaking, inconsistent.

bib.abstract: The impact of trades on asset prices is a crucial aspect of market dynamics for academics, regulators, and practitioners alike. Recently, universal and highly nonlinear master curves were observed for price impacts aggregated on all intra-day scales (Patzelt and Bouchaud 2017 arXiv:1706.04163). Here we investigate how well these curves, their scaling, and the underlying return dynamics are captured by linear ‘propagator’ models. We find that the classification of trades as price-changing versus non-price-changing can explain the price impact nonlinearities and short-term return dynamics to a very high degree. The explanatory power provided by the change indicator in addition to the order sign history increases with increasing tick size. To obtain these results, several long-standing technical issues for model calibration and testing are addressed. We present new spectral estimators for two- and three-point cross-correlations, removing the need for previously used approximations. We also show when calibration is unbiased and how to accurately reveal previously overlooked biases. Therefore, our results contribute significantly to understanding both recent empirical results and the properties of a popular class of impact models.

bib.abstract: The trading activity in the German intraday electricity market has increased significantly over the last years. This is partially due to an increasing share of renewable energy, wind and photovoltaic, which requires power generators to balance out the forecasting errors in their production. We investigate the bidding behaviour in the intraday market by looking at both last prices and continuous bidding, in the context of a reduced-form econometric analysis. A unique data set of 15-minute intraday prices and intraday-updated forecasts of wind and photovoltaic has been employed. Price bids are explained by prior information on renewables forecasts and demand/supply market-specific exogenous variables. We show that intraday prices adjust asymmetrically to both forecasting errors in renewables and to the volume of trades dependent on the threshold variable demand quote, which reflects the expected demand covered by the planned traditional capacity in the day-ahead market. The location of the threshold can be used by market participants to adjust their bids accordingly, given the latest updates in the wind and photovoltaic forecasting errors and the forecasts of the control area balances.
